extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, IP counsel, patent examiners, and stakeholders drafting or evaluating AI-related patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting patent claims for AI-related inventions under USPTO subject matter eligibility guidance (Alice/Mayo framework), with practical drafting considerations and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply MPEP 2103-2106.07(c) combined eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s subject matter eligibility guidance, found in the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) sections 2103-2106.07(c), applies to all technologies, including AI inventions. The guidance combines the criteria for eligibility into a single analysis addressing statutory categories and judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the MPEP framework to determine whether a claim falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether it is directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). Apply the combined/single analysis consistently to AI-related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A, Prong One — does the claim recite an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea as the first part of the Step 2A Alice/Mayo inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claim limitations map to judicially-recognized abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes). If the claim recites an abstract idea, proceed to Prong Two; if not, eligibility can be found at this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A, Prong Two — integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application, i.e., whether it applies the exception in a way that produces a technical improvement or practical implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prong Two is satisfied when the claim shows that the abstract idea is applied in conjunction with particular machines/techniques or otherwise improves the functioning of a computer or other technology. Mere use of a generic computer or generic ML model is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'involves' vs 'recites' an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between claims that merely involve an abstract idea and those that recite an abstract idea, because the latter require further eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely involve abstract ideas may be treated as per se eligible, whereas claims that recite the judicial exception must undergo the Alice/Mayo.Step 2A analysis. Drafting should aim to avoid language that causes a claim to be characterized as reciting an abstract idea when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize groupings of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are grouped by the USPTO into mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing claims, map limitations to these groupings to determine if an abstract idea is present (e.g., feature extraction/comparison may be a 'mental process' or 'mathematical concept'). Use this mapping to anticipate Step 2A outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware-specific or physical-device claims are more likely eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite specific hardware or physical structures (e.g., an ASIC with a particular neuronal array and synaptic circuits) can be found eligible as falling within a statutory category (machine) and not reciting a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to include concrete physical components or device structures where appropriate; emphasize physical architecture to support eligibility at Step 1 and Prong One analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve computer or other technology support practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A key consideration for eligibility is whether the claim demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the claimed invention provides a particular solution to a problem or a specific way to achieve a desired outcome (e.g., rule-based system improving animation processes). Emphasize technical improvements rather than abstract goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming merely the use of a generic computer or generic ML model
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply instruct to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer component or a generic machine learning model are often ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance cites examples where methods that rely on a generic machine learning model to perform an abstract process were found ineligible as 'mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component.' To avoid this anti-pattern, include technical specifics about implementation, structure, or training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add specific technical details (structure, training, implementation) to support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding claim limitations that recite specific architectures, training techniques, data discretization methods, or implementation details can transform an otherwise ineligible claim into an eligible one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that claims which recite a particular manner of training/using a neural network, a particular neural network architecture, or specific implementation details were found to integrate the abstract idea into a practical application. Include such specifics in claims and specification where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'meaningful limits' in claim scope (practical/particular limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include meaningful, particular limits (e.g., a recited specific compound in a treatment) are more likely to be viewed as practical applications rather than abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, narrow claims by reciting particular compounds, steps, or contextual limits that tie the claim to a concrete application or improvement in technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus claim drafting on specific solutions, not abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should describe a particular solution or a specific way to achieve the desired outcome rather than broadly claiming the idea of the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize actionable technical steps, device features, or trained-model particulars that show how the invention achieves the result. Avoid high-level goal language that merely states an objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document technological improvements in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should clearly describe how the claimed invention improves existing technological processes to support a practical application finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe technical advantages, improvements to computer functionality or other technology, and concrete implementation details in the written description to help overcome eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of invention creation (use of AI) is not relevant to subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether AI was used to create the invention is not considered in the subject matter eligibility analysis; the guidance focuses on claim language and technical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on or argue eligibility based on the fact that AI assisted in conception; instead, ground eligibility arguments in claim limitations and technical improvements recited in the claim and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship for AI-assisted inventions — human contributors must be documented
rubrics_metrics.description: While AI use does not affect subject matter eligibility, inventorship remains statutory and current statutes do not recognize AI systems as inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that one or more natural persons who made significant contributions to the claimed invention are identified and that their contributions are documented in prosecution materials and internal records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage USPTO examples and monitor case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the USPTO’s new eligibility examples (Examples 47–49) and prior examples to frame claims and prosecution strategies, and stay current with Federal Circuit decisions interpreting eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the provided examples (e.g., ASIC for ANN, discretization and ANN anomaly detection, speech signal processing, personalized medical treatment examples) to model claim drafting and anticipate examiner analysis; keep abreast of court decisions for evolving interpretations.
